Overview

Younger Bloomington residents faced low awareness of planning meetings and proposals that were hard to picture. My HCI/d capstone explored a mobile way to understand neighborhood projects and contribute ideas.

Resident and planner research led to a simulated neighborhood, ready-made design elements, and proposal feedback. The current prototype adds a categorized builder and progress updates; six residents tested the original 2025 concept.

Key Impact

6 residents tested the concept

Participants saw potential for inclusive community engagement and identified two usability refinements. This is qualitative feedback on the 2025 prototype; participation growth and the current revision’s usability remain unmeasured.

A public meeting only works if people can take part.

My research in Bloomington pointed to low awareness of planning meetings, inconvenient participation methods, and proposals that were difficult to picture in context. Younger residents were often missing from the conversation.

I narrowed an initially broad urban-design problem to Bloomington community projects and residents aged 18–35. That focus made the concept specific enough to test.

Listen to both sides of participation.

The capstone combined secondary research and digital ethnography with resident and planning interviews. A participatory workshop helped explore three directions: a collaborative kiosk, an AR app, and a simulated neighborhood.

Paper concepts were also compared with 2 city planners and 2 users. These are activity-specific counts; participant overlap is unconfirmed.

See the place before judging the proposal.

I chose the simulation direction to connect exploration, feedback, and resident-made proposals. A map gives changes a spatial context; project details explain their purpose and constraints.

On mobile, a draggable bottom sheet snaps between collapsed, middle, and expanded states, balancing the map with project information. Bottom navigation keeps Explore, Proposals, My activity, and Notifications within reach.

Search, zoom, and a simulated street view support exploration. Project dates, contacts, and dimensions remain explicitly unconfirmed.

Give people a starting point for their ideas.

Ready-made elements let residents suggest a use for a space without drawing a plan from scratch. A bounded library offers an approachable starting point, with less freedom than a full design tool.

Residents browse Buildings, Outdoors, and Mobility, then drag an element onto the plot—or select and tap to place it. They can adjust or remove elements, save a draft, and review their idea before a mock submission.

Keep participation going after “submit.”

A resident needs to know what happens to an idea. Notifications brings together an acknowledgment, reference number, next step, and progress tracker for their proposal.

Residents can also follow proposals they voted on or commented on. Dedicated proposal views make room for feedback without competing with the map.

Committee messages, votes, and review stages are mock data. They demonstrate the flow, not community consensus or real planning decisions.

What testing revealed—and what still needs testing.

Six Bloomington residents tested the 2025 high-fidelity prototype. They saw it as a valuable, inclusive way to engage with community projects and identified two usability refinements.

Finding 01

Make elements easier to choose.

Participants needed clearer categories in the builder. The current app now groups elements by function; its effect on usability still needs testing.

Finding 02

Make the result easy to notice.

A proposed design’s arrival in the plot needed more emphasis. The current app provides placement feedback and a submission preview; whether these resolve the original issue is untested.

The original findings support the concept’s potential, not city-wide adoption or improved participation. The current interactive version is a later prototype, not the artifact tested in 2025.

Try Block Party

Try the mobile app in a phone-sized preview, or open it in a new tab. Activity stays in your browser; city views, committee messages, and review stages are simulated. Proposals are not sent to the council.

An inviting interface is only part of inclusion.

Architecture taught me to think about how a place affects everyday life. This project pushed me to ask whose experience reaches a planning decision—and whose is missing.

Next, I would test the revised builder and progress flow with residents of different digital confidence levels, then work with planners on interpreting conflicting input. A digital channel needs outreach and a credible review process before it can represent a community.
